title: Cellular Processes: Metabolism
summary: In this lesson students learn how cells obtain energy through photosynthesis and cellular respiration. They compare the two processes and see how they are linked in the flow of energy in living organisms.
objectives: Explain the overall equation of photosynthesis and identify its reactants and products
Describe the main stages of cellular respiration and their purpose
Compare and contrast where and how energy is stored and released in both processes
Illustrate how the products of photosynthesis become the reactants of respiration
prerequisites: Students should already know basic cell structure, including the presence of chloroplasts and mitochondria.
why: Energy flow is the foundation of all life. Understanding photosynthesis shows how plants capture sunlight and turn it into chemical energy that fuels ecosystems.

Cellular respiration explains how that stored energy is released for growth, movement, and maintenance in all organisms, including humans. This knowledge underpins nutrition, agriculture, and climate science.

sections.heading: What is Energy in Biology?
sections.body:
Energy is what lets a cell do anything at all – grow, move, divide, or simply keep its doors closed so that the inside stays safe.  
In biology we usually talk about **chemical energy**, which is stored in the bonds between atoms inside molecules. When those bonds are broken or rearranged, the stored energy can be released and used for work, just like a spring releases its stored tension when it snaps back.

> **Definition:** *Chemical energy* – the potential energy stored in the chemical bonds of a molecule. It becomes available when the bonds are broken or re‑formed during a chemical reaction.

The most important carrier of chemical energy in every living cell is a tiny molecule called **adenosine triphosphate**, abbreviated **ATP**. ATP looks complicated, but you can think of it as a small battery. It has three phosphate groups attached in a chain; the link between the second and third phosphate is especially high‑energy. When the cell cuts off that third phosphate, the bond breaks and a lot of energy is released.

The reaction can be written as  

$$\text{ATP} \;\rightarrow\; \text{ADP} + \text{P}_i + \text{energy}$$  

where **ADP** stands for adenosine diphosphate (the same molecule with only two phosphates) and **P**\(_i\) is an inorganic phosphate. The cell then uses the released energy to power processes such as moving proteins, synthesizing new molecules, or pumping ions across membranes.

> **Note:** The energy released from ATP is not a flame or heat that the cell feels; it is used directly to change the shape or activity of other proteins, acting like a molecular “on‑switch”.

Why does a cell need this energy? Imagine trying to push a heavy box across a floor. If you just stand still, the box won’t move. You must apply a force over a distance – that is **work** in physics. In a cell, “work” includes many microscopic tasks: a motor protein dragging a vesicle along a filament, an enzyme joining two smaller molecules into a larger one, or a membrane pump moving sodium ions out while potassium ions move in. All of these require an input of energy, otherwise the cell would be stuck in a static state.

> **In daily life:** Think of ATP as the money in a wallet. Your body earns money (energy) by eating food, then spends it on different activities – walking, thinking, heating your home. If the wallet is empty, you can’t buy anything. Similarly, a cell without ATP cannot “pay” for its work.

How does a cell obtain ATP? The answer lies in two larger processes – photosynthesis (in plants) and cellular respiration (in all organisms). Both are series of chemical reactions that convert the energy stored in sunlight or in food molecules into the high‑energy phosphate bond of ATP. The important point is that the cell never creates energy from nothing; it only transforms it from one form to another, obeying the law of conservation of energy.

> **Common mistake:** Some textbooks say ATP “stores energy”. It is more accurate to say ATP *carries* energy that was previously stored in the bonds of glucose or other fuel molecules. The ATP molecule itself does not generate energy; it simply provides a convenient way to move that energy to where it is needed.

Remember that every living thing, from a tiny bacterium to a towering tree, relies on this cycle of making, using, and recycling ATP. When you feel tired after a run, your muscles have used a lot of ATP and need to replenish it by breathing in oxygen and breaking down sugars – the same basic principle that powers a single cell.  

> **Remember:** Cells are tiny factories. ATP is the universal energy currency that lets them buy the “services” they need to stay alive and grow.

sections.heading: Overview of Photosynthesis
sections.body:
Photosynthesis is the way green plants, algae, and some bacteria turn light from the sun into chemical energy that they can store and use later.  
In plain words, it is a **conversion process**: light energy → sugar (glucose) + oxygen.  
The reason this matters is that almost all life on Earth depends on the food and oxygen that photosynthesis creates. Without it, the food chain would collapse and the air would lack the oxygen we breathe.

The overall chemical equation for photosynthesis is  

$$6\;CO_2 \;+\;6\;H_2O \;+\;light\;energy \;\rightarrow\; C_6H_{12}O_6 \;+\;6\;O_2$$  

Let’s break down each part of this equation.

**Carbon dioxide ($CO_2$)** is a gas that plants take in from the air through tiny openings on their leaves called *stomata*.  
**Water ($H_2O$)** is absorbed by the roots and travels up the plant’s vascular system to the leaves.  
**Light energy** comes from sunlight; the pigment *chlorophyll* in the leaf cells captures this energy.  
All three of these inputs are combined inside structures called *chloroplasts* to produce **glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$)**, a simple sugar that stores energy, and **oxygen ($O_2$)**, which is released back into the atmosphere.

Why does sunlight matter? Sunlight provides the energy needed to break the stable bonds in carbon dioxide and water. Think of it like a child using a battery‑powered flashlight to melt ice cubes. The light supplies the power that lets the plant rearrange the atoms into new molecules.

The glucose that is made is not just a sweet treat; it is the plant’s fuel. The plant can use glucose immediately for growth, repair, and reproduction, or it can store it as starch for later use—much like how we store food in a pantry for days when we cannot cook. When animals (including humans) eat plants, they obtain the stored energy in the form of glucose, and they also get the oxygen that plants have released.

> **Note:** The equation shows *six* molecules of carbon dioxide and *six* molecules of water because each glucose molecule contains six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogen atoms, and six oxygen atoms. The numbers balance so that atoms are neither created nor destroyed, obeying the law of conservation of mass.

A useful everyday comparison is a solar panel on a house. The panel captures sunlight and turns it into electricity that powers appliances. In photosynthesis, the leaf is the solar panel, sunlight is the electricity, and the “appliance” is the plant’s metabolism that uses glucose as its energy source.

It is important to remember that photosynthesis occurs in two main stages: the *light‑dependent reactions* (where sunlight splits water and creates a high‑energy carrier) and the *Calvin cycle* (where carbon dioxide is fixed into glucose). Although we will study those stages later, the overall picture remains the same: light + water + carbon dioxide → sugar + oxygen.

> **In daily life:** The oxygen you breathe and the food you eat both start with this single process. Every leaf on a tree, every blade of grass, and every algae cell in a pond is performing the same reaction that keeps the planet alive.

> **Common mistake:** Some textbooks write the equation backwards, showing glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + light energy. That is actually the reverse process—*cellular respiration*—which occurs in animals and also in plant cells when they need energy. Remember, photosynthesis builds glucose; respiration breaks it down.

In summary, photosynthesis captures solar energy, combines it with water and carbon dioxide, and produces glucose (a usable energy store) and oxygen (a vital gas for many organisms). Understanding this simple equation gives insight into the flow of energy through ecosystems and the essential role of the Sun in life on Earth.

sections.heading: Key Steps of Photosynthesis
sections.body:
Photosynthesis is the way green plants, algae, and some bacteria turn light energy into chemical energy that can be used for growth.  
Think of it as a tiny factory inside each chloroplast (the green organelle in a leaf). The factory has two main assembly lines: the **light‑dependent reactions** and the **Calvin cycle**.  

First, the light‑dependent reactions are like solar panels on a roof. They capture sunlight and turn it into a short‑lived energy carrier called **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) and a stable carrier called **NADPH** (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate).  
- **Chlorophyll**, the green pigment, absorbs photons (particles of light). When a photon hits chlorophyll, an electron inside the pigment gets excited – it jumps to a higher energy level.  
- The excited electron is passed along a series of proteins embedded in the thylakoid membrane; this series is called the **electron transport chain**. As the electron moves, it releases energy that pumps protons (hydrogen ions, H⁺) across the membrane, creating a gradient.  
- The flow of protons back through a protein called **ATP synthase** spins the protein like a turbine, making ATP from ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and a phosphate group.  
- Meanwhile, the electron finally reaches a molecule called **NADP⁺**, which picks up the electron and a hydrogen ion to become NADPH.  

> **Definition:** *Photon* – a tiny packet of light energy that can raise an electron to a higher energy level.  

The overall light‑dependent reaction can be written as  

$$
2 \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2 \text{NADP}^+ + 3 \text{ADP} + 3 \text{P}_i + \text{light} \rightarrow O_2 + 2 \text{NADPH} + 3 \text{ATP}
$$  

Here water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is split, releasing oxygen ($O_2$) as a waste product, and the energy captured ends up in ATP and NADPH.

Now the Calvin cycle is the second assembly line, working in the stroma (the fluid surrounding the thylakoids). Its job is **carbon fixation** – taking carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) from the air and turning it into a sugar called **glucose**. The cycle uses the ATP and NADPH made in the first stage, just like a bakery uses electricity and flour to bake bread.  

The Calvin cycle has three main steps, repeated over and over:

1. **Carbon fixation** – An enzyme called **Rubisco** (ribulose‑1,5‑bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) grabs a $CO_2$ molecule and attaches it to a five‑carbon sugar named ribulose‑1,5‑bisphosphate (RuBP). This creates an unstable six‑carbon compound that instantly splits into two three‑carbon molecules called 3‑phosphoglycerate (3‑PGA).  
2. **Reduction** – Each 3‑PGA receives an electron and a hydrogen from NADPH, and a phosphate from ATP, turning into glyceraldehyde‑3‑phosphate (G3P). Some G3P molecules leave the cycle and are later linked together to form glucose and other carbohydrates.  
3. **Regeneration** – The remaining G3P molecules are rearranged, using more ATP, to rebuild RuBP, allowing the cycle to start again with another $CO_2$.

> **Note:** The Calvin cycle does **not** need light directly, but it depends on the ATP and NADPH that the light‑dependent reactions produce.  

Putting the two parts together, the plant first harvests light energy, stores it in ATP and NADPH, then uses that stored energy to stitch carbon atoms from $CO_2$ into sugar molecules. This sugar can be broken down later to release energy for the plant’s own needs, or it can be stored as starch, cellulose, or other useful compounds.

> **In daily life:** The sugar made by the Calvin cycle is the source of the food we eat—fruits, vegetables, grains—and the oxygen released during the light‑dependent reactions is the air we breathe.  

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that the Calvin cycle needs light itself. It only needs the products of the light‑dependent reactions; the two stages happen in different parts of the chloroplast and can even occur at slightly different times of day.  

Remember that photosynthesis is a two‑step process: capture light → make energy carriers, then use those carriers to turn carbon dioxide into sugar. This simple division helps scientists study each part separately and understand how plants power the whole biosphere.

sections.heading: Overview of Cellular Respiration
sections.body:
Cellular respiration is the way a cell turns the sugar it has eaten into usable energy.  
In plain words, it is a set of chemical reactions that break down glucose (a simple sugar) while using oxygen, and the result is carbon dioxide, water, and a lot of tiny energy packets called **ATP** (adenosine‑triphosphate). ATP works like a rechargeable battery that powers almost every activity inside the cell, from moving muscles to copying DNA.

Why does this matter?  
All living things need energy to stay alive, grow, and reproduce. By understanding how cells get that energy, we can see how food we eat becomes the fuel for our bodies, and why we need to breathe oxygen.

The overall chemical equation that summarizes cellular respiration is:

$$
C_6H_{12}O_6 \;+\; 6\,O_2 \;\longrightarrow\; 6\,CO_2 \;+\; 6\,H_2O \;+\; \approx 38\,ATP
$$

* **Glucose** ($C_6H_{12}O_6$) is the sugar molecule that comes from the food we eat.  
* **Oxygen** ($O_2$) is the gas we inhale.  
* **Carbon dioxide** ($CO_2$) and **water** ($H_2O$) are waste products that we exhale or excrete.  
* **ATP** is the energy currency that the cell can immediately use.

> **Definition:** *Cellular respiration* – a series of metabolic pathways that convert biochemical energy from nutrients into ATP, and release waste products.

### Step‑by‑step picture

1. **Glycolysis** – This first stage happens in the fluid part of the cell (the cytoplasm). One glucose molecule is split into two smaller pieces called pyruvate. A small amount of ATP is made directly, and some carrier molecules called NAD⁺ pick up electrons and become NADH. Think of glycolysis as a quick, low‑power “starter” that gets the process going, similar to a car’s starter motor turning the engine over.

2. **Link reaction (pyruvate oxidation)** – The pyruvate molecules move into the mitochondrion, the cell’s “power plant.” Here each pyruvate loses a carbon atom, turning into a two‑carbon molecule called acetyl‑CoA. More NADH is produced and carbon dioxide is released as a waste gas.

3. **Citric Acid Cycle (Krebs cycle)** – Acetyl‑CoA enters a circular series of reactions. Each turn of the cycle releases two more carbon dioxide molecules, makes more NADH and another carrier called FADH₂, and produces a tiny amount of ATP directly. The cycle is like a recycling loop that extracts every possible bit of energy from the carbon skeleton of glucose.

4. **Electron Transport Chain (ETC) and Oxidative Phosphorylation** – This is the grand finale, occurring in the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. The NADH and FADH₂ from earlier steps donate their high‑energy electrons to a chain of protein complexes. As electrons move down the chain, energy is used to pump protons (H⁺ ions) across the membrane, creating a gradient—much like water stored behind a dam. The flow of protons back through a protein called ATP synthase drives the synthesis of the majority of ATP (about 34‑36 molecules). At the end of the chain, the electrons combine with oxygen and protons to form water, which is why we need oxygen to complete the process.

> **Note:** Oxygen is the final “electron acceptor” in the ETC. Without it, the chain backs up, NADH and FADH₂ cannot be regenerated, and ATP production stops. This is why cells die quickly when oxygen is absent.

### Everyday comparison

Imagine a bakery that receives a sack of flour (glucose). The baker first splits the flour into smaller portions (glycolysis) to start making dough. The dough is then sent to a special oven (mitochondrion) where it is baked in stages, releasing steam (CO₂) and heat (energy). The heat powers a set of machines that package the baked goods into ready‑to‑eat slices (ATP). The oven needs a steady supply of fresh air (oxygen) to keep the fire burning; without it, the bakery stalls.

> **In daily life:** When you run, your muscles need ATP quickly. They first use the ATP already stored, then break down glucose without oxygen (anaerobic respiration) for a short burst, and finally rely on the full aerobic respiration described above for sustained energy.

### Key take‑away

Cellular respiration is the cell’s method of turning the chemical energy stored in glucose, with the help of oxygen, into ATP, while releasing carbon dioxide and water as waste. This process powers everything from a single‑cell organism’s movement to a human’s marathon run. Understanding each step helps us see why breathing, eating, and staying active are all linked through this fundamental biological engine.

sections.heading: Stages of Cellular Respiration
sections.body:
Cellular respiration is the way a cell turns the sugar it gets from food into usable energy, called **ATP** (adenosine‑triphosphate). Think of ATP as a tiny rechargeable battery that powers almost everything a cell does – from moving muscles to copying DNA. The whole process happens in three main stages: **glycolysis**, the **Krebs cycle**, and **oxidative phosphorylation**. We will look at each stage, see what happens, and find out where most of the ATP is actually made.

**1. Glycolysis – the quick start**  
Glycolysis (pronounced “guy‑koh‑lee‑sis”) means “splitting sugar.” It takes place in the fluid part of the cell called the cytoplasm, so it does not need any special compartments. One molecule of glucose (a six‑carbon sugar) is broken down into two molecules of pyruvate (each with three carbons).  

During this breakdown, the cell invests a little energy first – it uses **2 ATP** to add phosphate groups to glucose, making the molecule more reactive. Then, through a series of enzyme‑catalyzed steps, the cell harvests energy and produces **4 ATP** and **2 NADH** (another energy‑carrying molecule). The net gain from glycolysis is therefore **2 ATP** and **2 NADH** per glucose.

> **Note:** Glycolysis does not need oxygen, so it can run whether the cell is in an aerobic (with oxygen) or anaerobic (without oxygen) environment.

**2. The Krebs Cycle – the “energy‑factory”**  
Also called the citric acid cycle or TCA cycle, the Krebs cycle takes place inside the mitochondrion, specifically in the matrix (the innermost space). Before entering the cycle, each pyruvate from glycolysis is changed into a molecule called **acetyl‑CoA**; this step releases **1 CO₂** and creates **1 NADH** per pyruvate (so 2 NADH per original glucose).

The acetyl‑CoA then combines with a four‑carbon molecule and goes through a circular series of reactions. For each turn of the cycle (and there are two turns per glucose), the cell produces:

- **3 NADH**
- **1 FADH₂** (another carrier similar to NADH)
- **1 GTP**, which is quickly converted to **ATP**
- **2 CO₂** as waste

Summing the two turns, the Krebs cycle yields **6 NADH**, **2 FADH₂**, **2 ATP**, and releases **4 CO₂**.

> **Definition:** NADH and FADH₂ are “electron carriers.” They pick up high‑energy electrons during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle and later give those electrons to the next stage, oxidative phosphorylation.

**3. Oxidative Phosphorylation – the big ATP maker**  
This final stage happens on the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. It has two linked parts: the **electron transport chain (ETC)** and **chemiosmosis**.

- **Electron transport chain:** NADH and FADH₂ dump their electrons onto a series of protein complexes embedded in the membrane. As electrons move down the chain, the energy they release is used to pump protons (H⁺ ions) from the matrix to the space between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes. This creates a proton gradient, like water stored behind a dam.

- **Chemiosmosis:** Protons flow back into the matrix through a protein called **ATP synthase**. The flow of protons turns this enzyme like a turbine, and the mechanical energy is used to attach a phosphate group to ADP (adenosine‑diphosphate), forming **ATP**.

The amount of ATP made depends on how many NADH and FADH₂ enter the ETC. Roughly:

$$
\text{From each NADH} \approx 2.5 \text{ ATP} \\
\text{From each FADH}_2 \approx 1.5 \text{ ATP}
$$

Putting the numbers together for one glucose molecule:

- Glycolysis provides **2 NADH** → about **5 ATP**
- Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA gives **2 NADH** → about **5 ATP**
- Krebs cycle gives **6 NADH** → about **15 ATP**
- Krebs cycle gives **2 FADH₂** → about **3 ATP**
- Direct substrate‑level phosphorylation (2 ATP from glycolysis + 2 ATP from the Krebs cycle) → **4 ATP**

Total ≈ **32 ATP** per glucose, with **about 26–28 ATP** coming from oxidative phosphorylation. This means **most of the cell’s usable energy is produced in the last stage**, not in glycolysis or the Krebs cycle.

> **In daily life:** Think of glycolysis as the starter motor of a car – it gets things moving quickly but doesn’t produce much power. The Krebs cycle is the engine’s combustion chambers, generating a lot of fuel (NADH, FADH₂). Oxidative phosphorylation is the turbocharger that turns that fuel into the actual horsepower (ATP) that drives the car forward.

**Why this matters**  
Understanding where ATP is made helps us see why oxygen is so important. Without oxygen, the electron transport chain can’t operate, and the cell must rely only on glycolysis, which yields a tiny 2 ATP per glucose. That’s why muscles tire quickly during intense exercise when oxygen supply is limited.

> **Remember:** The bulk of ATP (≈80 %) comes from oxidative phosphorylation, the stage that needs oxygen and the inner mitochondrial membrane’s “dam” to create a proton gradient.

sections.heading: Linking the Two Processes
sections.body:
Plants, algae, and some bacteria capture sunlight and turn it into chemical energy through **photosynthesis**. Animals, fungi, and most microbes break down that stored chemical energy to do work in a process called **cellular respiration**. The two pathways are like the two halves of a circle: the output of one becomes the input of the other, keeping the flow of energy and matter continuous in ecosystems.

First, remember the overall equation for photosynthesis:

$$
6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \;\xrightarrow{\text{light}}\; \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2
$$

Carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air and water (H₂O) from the soil are combined using light energy to make glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) and oxygen (O₂). Glucose is a simple sugar that stores energy in its chemical bonds; oxygen is released back into the atmosphere.

When a living cell needs energy, it performs cellular respiration, which can be summarized by the reverse equation:

$$
\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2 \;\xrightarrow{\text{oxidation}}\; 6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{energy (ATP)}
$$

Here the same glucose molecule is broken down, and the oxygen produced in photosynthesis is used as the final electron acceptor. The breakdown releases carbon dioxide, water, and usable energy in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the cell’s “energy currency”.

> **Definition:** **ATP** – a small molecule that stores and transports chemical energy within cells. One ATP molecule can power many cellular activities, such as muscle contraction, nerve signaling, and synthesis of new molecules.

The link between the two processes works at several levels:

1. **Molecular link** – The glucose made in photosynthesis is the exact fuel that respiration consumes. Likewise, the O₂ released by photosynthesis is the same O₂ that respiration needs to accept electrons. When glucose is oxidized, the carbon atoms end up as CO₂, which photosynthetic organisms can capture again.

2. **Energy link** – The energy stored in the bonds of glucose (about 2800 kJ per mole) is released during respiration. Most of this energy is captured in ATP; a small fraction is lost as heat, which helps maintain body temperature in animals.

3. **Ecological link** – In a forest, trees (photosynthesizers) produce O₂ and glucose. Herbivores eat the leaves, obtaining glucose for respiration. Their waste and breath release CO₂, which the trees use again. This recycling keeps the atmosphere’s O₂ and CO₂ levels relatively stable over long periods.

> **In daily life:** Think of a kitchen. Photosynthesis is like a chef preparing a batch of soup (glucose) and spilling some steam (O₂) into the room. Respiration is a family eating the soup; they exhale the steam (CO₂) and produce heat (energy). The kitchen’s ventilation system (the atmosphere) carries the steam back to the chef, who can use it to make more soup.

Because the two processes are tightly coupled, a change in one affects the other. If a plant is shaded and cannot perform photosynthesis efficiently, it produces less glucose and O₂. Animals that rely on that plant will have less food and less O₂ to breathe, which can lower their respiration rates. Conversely, if an animal population grows very large, it releases more CO₂, which can stimulate photosynthetic activity—provided there is enough light and water.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that plants “breathe” the same way animals do. Plants do respire, but they also perform photosynthesis. During daylight, photosynthesis usually dominates, so plants take in more CO₂ than they release. At night, without light, they only respire, releasing CO₂.

Finally, the balance between photosynthesis and respiration is essential for the global carbon cycle. Human activities that burn fossil fuels add extra CO₂ to the atmosphere, overwhelming the natural capacity of photosynthesizers to convert it back into glucose. Understanding the link helps us see why protecting forests and promoting plant growth are key strategies for mitigating climate change.

> **Remember:** The products of photosynthesis (glucose and O₂) are the raw materials for respiration, and the waste products of respiration (CO₂ and H₂O) are the raw materials for photosynthesis. This circular flow keeps energy moving through living systems.

sections.heading: Real‑World Connections
sections.body:
Plants, animals, and even tiny microbes all need energy to live. The way they get that energy is through the two processes you have just studied: **photosynthesis** (which stores energy in sugar) and **cellular respiration** (which releases that energy for work). Let’s see how these ideas show up in the world around us.

First, think about a garden. When a seed sprouts, the tiny leaf cells begin to capture sunlight. They use photosynthesis to turn carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil into glucose, a simple sugar. The reaction can be written as  

$$\text{6 CO}_2 + \text{6 H}_2\text{O} + \text{light energy} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + \text{6 O}_2$$  

The glucose is the plant’s “food.” As the plant grows, it breaks down that glucose in its cells through cellular respiration:

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + \text{6 O}_2 \rightarrow \text{6 CO}_2 + \text{6 H}_2\text{O} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$  

The energy released (in the form of a molecule called ATP) powers everything the plant does: making new cells, stretching roots deeper, and producing fruits or flowers.  

> **In daily life:** The fruit you eat, the wood used to build a house, and the cotton in your shirt all started as glucose made by photosynthesis and later used in respiration.

Now imagine a human eating that fruit. The sugar you digest is chemically the same glucose the plant made. Your body’s cells take the glucose into mitochondria, the “power plants” of the cell, and run cellular respiration. The ATP produced fuels muscle contraction when you run, nerve signals when you think, and even the tiny pumps that keep your heart beating.  

> **Definition:** *ATP* (adenosine triphosphate) is the immediate energy currency of cells; one ATP molecule can power many small tasks, but it is quickly used up and must be regenerated by respiration.

Because the same molecule (glucose) is the link between plants and animals, the two processes together create a **carbon cycle**. Carbon atoms travel from the atmosphere (as CO₂) into plants, then into animals that eat the plants, and back into the atmosphere when we exhale or when plants and animals decompose. This cycle keeps the amount of carbon in the Earth’s systems relatively stable.  

> **Note:** The carbon cycle is not a one‑way street; it moves in loops. When a forest is cut down, the loop is broken, and excess CO₂ can stay in the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.

A practical example is the use of biofuels. Scientists grow algae or crops that are rich in sugars or oils. By harvesting these organisms and processing their stored energy, we obtain fuels that can replace gasoline. The fuel is essentially the stored glucose (or a derivative) that was made by photosynthesis. When the biofuel is burned in an engine, it undergoes a form of respiration, releasing CO₂ that the original plants had taken from the air. In theory, the CO₂ released is “balanced” by the CO₂ the plants removed, making the fuel carbon‑neutral.  

> **Remember:** Carbon‑neutral does not mean no impact; growing crops for fuel still uses land, water, and fertilizers, which have their own environmental footprints.

Finally, think about everyday objects like paper. Paper is made from wood, which is made of cellulose—a long chain of glucose molecules. When you recycle paper, you are essentially returning carbon that was once in the atmosphere back into the cycle, rather than letting it sit in a landfill where it might decompose slowly and release methane, a potent greenhouse gas.  

In summary, the chemistry of photosynthesis and respiration is not confined to a textbook. It explains why plants grow tall, why we feel energetic after a meal, and how the Earth’s climate stays in balance. Understanding these connections helps us make better choices—whether it’s planting trees, eating a balanced diet, or supporting sustainable energy—because we see the direct link between tiny cellular reactions and the big world we live in.

practice.q: What is the role of sunlight in photosynthesis?
practice.a: Sunlight provides the energy needed to drive the light‑dependent reactions. Chlorophyll absorbs photons, which excite electrons. These high‑energy electrons help split water molecules and generate ATP and NADPH, the energy carriers used later to make glucose.

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) stores chemical energy in its high‑energy phosphate bonds. When a cell needs energy for tasks such as muscle contraction, active transport, or biosynthesis, it hydrolyzes ATP to ADP + Pi, releasing energy that powers those processes.

practice.q: Compare where the energy‑carrier molecules NADPH and ATP are produced in photosynthesis and where they are used in cellular respiration.
practice.a: In photosynthesis, NADPH and ATP are made during the light‑dependent reactions in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. They are then used in the Calvin cycle (light‑independent reactions) to reduce CO₂ into glucose. In cellular respiration, NADH and ATP are produced during glycolysis (cytoplasm) and the citric‑acid cycle (mitochondrial matrix). NADH then donates electrons to the electron‑transport chain, where most ATP is generated by oxidative phosphorylation in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

practice.q: Explain how the products of photosynthesis become the reactants for cellular respiration.
practice.a: Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. The glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the main fuel for cellular respiration, and the oxygen (O₂) is the final electron acceptor in the electron‑transport chain. During respiration, glucose is broken down back into CO₂ and H₂O, releasing energy stored in its bonds.

practice.q: A plant leaf produces 120 J of chemical energy in glucose during one hour of light. If the leaf’s mitochondria use 30 J of that energy per hour for cellular respiration, what percentage of the photosynthetic energy is immediately available for the plant’s growth and other non‑respiratory functions?
practice.a: First, determine the amount of energy not used for respiration: 120 J (produced) – 30 J (used in respiration) = 90 J. Next, calculate the percentage of the original 120 J that 90 J represents: (90 J ÷ 120 J) × 100 % = 0.75 × 100 % = 75 %. Therefore, 75 % of the photosynthetic energy is available for growth and other functions.

practice.q: Describe how a defect in the enzyme ATP synthase would affect both photosynthesis and cellular respiration, and predict the observable consequences for a plant.
practice.a: ATP synthase makes ATP by allowing protons to flow back across a membrane (thylakoid membrane in chloroplasts, inner mitochondrial membrane in mitochondria). If ATP synthase is defective, the proton gradient cannot be used to synthesize ATP. In photosynthesis, the light‑dependent reactions would still generate NADPH and a proton gradient, but ATP production would be severely reduced, limiting the Calvin cycle’s ability to fix CO₂ into glucose. In cellular respiration, the electron‑transport chain would still pump protons, but without functional ATP synthase, oxidative phosphorylation would not produce ATP, forcing the cell to rely only on the small amount of ATP made by substrate‑level phosphorylation (glycolysis and citric‑acid cycle). For a plant, this would lead to very low glucose synthesis, stunted growth, yellowing leaves (chlorosis) due to energy shortage, and reduced ability to survive in the dark because respiration cannot supply enough ATP.

recap: Cells need energy to grow, move, and survive. Chemical energy is stored in molecular bonds and released when those bonds change, with ATP acting as the cell's battery. Photosynthesis captures sunlight to make glucose and oxygen, while cellular respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to produce CO₂, water, and ATP. Together these processes cycle energy through ecosystems.

key_terms.meaning: Potential energy stored in the bonds between atoms in a molecule.
A small molecule that stores and transfers energy in cells, often called the cellular battery.
The process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose) and release oxygen.
The set of reactions that break down glucose with oxygen to produce CO₂, water, and ATP.
The first stage of respiration that splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules, producing a small amount of ATP.
A series of reactions in the mitochondria that further breaks down pyruvate, releasing CO₂ and transferring energy to carrier molecules.
The final stage of respiration where most ATP is made using the electron transport chain and oxygen.
The set of reactions in the chloroplast that uses ATP and NADPH to turn CO₂ into glucose during photosynthesis.

quiz.q: What molecule directly provides energy for most cellular activities?
quiz.why: ATP is the immediate energy carrier used by cells.

quiz.q: During photosynthesis, which gas is taken in by plants?
quiz.why: Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air to make glucose.

quiz.q: Which stage of cellular respiration occurs in the cytoplasm?
quiz.why: Glycolysis takes place in the cell’s fluid (cytoplasm).

quiz.q: What is the main product of the light‑dependent reactions?
quiz.why: Light‑dependent reactions generate ATP and NADPH.

quiz.q: Which equation correctly represents cellular respiration?
quiz.why: Cellular respiration breaks glucose and oxygen into CO₂, water, and ATP.

quiz.q: In the Calvin cycle, which molecule is fixed to eventually become glucose?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide is incorporated (fixed) in the Calvin cycle to make sugar.

steps.label: Make Energy Carriers
steps.text: Produce ATP and NADPH in the light‑dependent reactions.

steps.label: Build Sugar
steps.text: Use ATP, NADPH, CO₂ in the Calvin cycle to form glucose.

steps.label: Glycolysis
steps.text: Glucose split into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm.

steps.label: Krebs Cycle
steps.text: Pyruvate is oxidized, releasing CO₂ and high‑energy electrons.

steps.label: Oxidative Phosphorylation
steps.text: Electrons drive ATP synthesis using oxygen as the final acceptor.
